query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals maintain their single‐phase solid solution at high operating temperatures (473–1923 K) when the high mixing entropy is complemented by significant lattice distortion that suppresses atomic diffusion, thereby counteracting tendencies for phase segregation or chemical ordering. In contrast, HEA nanoparticles with lower lattice distortion (i.e. smaller atomic size mismatches among constituents) will be more prone to diffusion‐driven phase separation under the same conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy nanoparticles synthesized as a single-phase solid solution with equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios of five or more metals.
generation.intervention: Select two HEA nanoparticle systems that initially share a similar equiatomic composition but differ in the atomic size mismatch of their constituent elements. One set is engineered with a larger spread in atomic sizes (thereby higher lattice distortion) while the comparison (control) set is chosen with elements having more similar atomic radii (lower lattice distortion).
generation.conditions: The nanoparticles are subjected to catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions in a controlled environment over a temperature range of 473–1923 K. All other variables—such as synthesis method, particle size, and initial phase—are held constant.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion and the resulting reduction in atomic diffusivity.
generation.mechanism: High mixing entropy stabilizes the solid solution, but the extent to which this stability is maintained at high temperatures depends on the kinetic barrier to atomic rearrangement. A higher lattice distortion (due to larger differences in atomic radii) increases energy barriers for atomic diffusion, thereby preserving the homogeneous, single-phase structure against temperature-induced phase separation or chemical ordering.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature catalytic/thermoelectric conditions, the HEA nanoparticles with larger atomic size mismatches (and thus higher lattice distortion) will display minimal changes in phase and composition relative to their as-synthesized solid solution state, while the control nanoparticles with lower lattice distortion will show measurable signs of phase segregation or chemical ordering.
generation.baseline: Initial as-synthesized single-phase, equiatomic HEA nanoparticles prior to high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to HEA nanoparticles synthesized under controlled conditions where the only major variable modified is the degree of atomic size mismatch. It assumes that other factors (e.g., precursor purity, synthesis kinetics, and particle size) are not significantly different between the tested groups.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative thresholds (e.g., the minimum atomic size mismatch required to sufficiently suppress diffusion) and the exact extent of phase separation in the low lattice distortion group remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles with identical equiatomic ratios but differing only in the selection of constituent metals to produce a high lattice distortion group and a low lattice distortion group. Subject both sets to prolonged catalytic/thermoelectric operation at temperatures ranging from 473 to 1923 K. Characterize the post-treatment phase and chemical homogeneity using XRD, TEM with EDS mapping, and surface-sensitive spectroscopies.
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns to detect emergence of secondary phases or peak splitting
Transmission electron microscopy imaging with elemental mapping to assess chemical ordering or segregation
Surface spectroscopy to detect changes in oxidation states or local site environments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both nanoparticle sets (high and low lattice distortion) exhibit similar levels of phase segregation, chemical ordering, or degradation relative to their initial single-phase state under the same operating conditions, then the hypothesized role of lattice distortion in governing high-temperature stability is not supported.

cited_evidence.text: The escalating issues of the energy crisis and environmental pollution underscore the urgency of the transition to a sustainable global economy. A pivotal aspect of this shift is the advancement of renewable energy technologies, especially those facilitating the conversion of chemical energy to electrical energy in fuel cells. At the heart of these energy conversion devices is the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), whose efficiency is considerably hindered by the dearth of effective electrocatalysts., Platinum (Pt) stands as the most effective pure metal catalyst for the ORR, yet its widespread application is constrained by its high cost and scarcity. Efforts to reduce the loading of precious metals while enhancing site-specific activity have concentrated on the modification of Pt sites with strategies such as defect engineering, core–shell nanostructuring, and near-surface alloying. A major limitation of these Pt-based site ensembles is long-term durability, severely compromised by interfacial processes such as leaching, dealloying, and degradation dynamically occurring under operating conditions. The newly-developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are receiving much attention for their unique structures and excellent properties,,,,,,,,,. Unlike traditional alloys, which are normally based on one or two principal elements, HEAs defined by Yeh et al. can have five or more principal elements in equal or near-equal molar ratios. In recent studies, quaternary and ternary alloys in an equal molar ratio are also considered as HEAs,. The presence of multiple principal elements in HEAs is not merely a difference in composition, but has fundamental physical effects on the configurational entropy, free energy, phase selection, and stability. In general, the high-entropy effect in these alloys can greatly reduce the free energy of simple solid-solution phases, especially at high temperatures, making the chemically-ordered intermetallic compounds less competitive. As a result, HEAs obtained after rapid quenching are often found to contain topologically-simple [e.g., face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC)] yet chemically-disordered solid solutions, nano-sized precipitates, and amorphous phases,,,.
